opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the big thing Freud got right, and it's easy to forget how radical it was at the time, is the idea that childhood matters: what happens to you when you're very young shapes who you become as an adult. Before Freud, there was a sense that children were just incomplete adults, and their experiences didn't really count for much. Freud said no, these early years are foundational. And I think the developmental science since then has broadly vindicated that intuition, even if not in the way he imagined.

The other thing he got right is that children have very rich inner lives. They have intense emotions, intense relationships, and a kind of wild, imaginative mental life that we as adults have largely lost access to. That's something I'd very much agree with.

Where he went wrong, I think, is in the specifics. He didn't actually watch children very much. Famously, most of his theories about childhood came from adults lying on a couch reconstructing their memories, and the one child case he did, Little Hans, was mediated through the father. So he had this picture of children as driven by irrational, sexual, aggressive urges that had to be tamed. What we've discovered, by actually doing experiments with babies and young children, is that they're much more like little scientists. They're rational in a deep sense. They're figuring out how the world works, how other people's minds work, testing hypotheses, learning from statistics. The irrationality Freud saw is often really exploration, which looks messy from the outside but is actually a very sophisticated learning strategy.

And the other piece, the attachment piece, comes more through Bowlby, who started out in the psychoanalytic tradition and then turned it into something empirical. The idea that the early relationship with caregivers gives you a kind of model of how relationships work, that's held up quite well. But it's less about repressed drives and more about children building theories, in this case, theories about love and the people around them.

So I'd say Freud asked the right questions and gave mostly the wrong answers, which is honestly not a bad legacy for a scientist.

r001.rationale: The response critiques Freud’s methods and theories but does not say he is largely absent from contemporary academic psychology.

r002.rationale: It says children learn how other minds work, but presents this as a finding of later developmental science, not as a Freudian intuition that held up.

r003.rationale: It says early experiences and caregiver relationships shape later life, but does not state that children’s inferences about their social world influence their subsequent development.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, not very much, honestly, at least not in the specific claims. The Oedipus complex, the psychosexual stages, oral and anal and all the rest of it — there's really no empirical support for any of that, and in some ways it was a very strange picture of what children are like. It was a picture of children as these little bundles of drives and conflicts, and that's just not what you see when you actually look carefully at what babies and young children are doing.

But I think there are a couple of things that did hold up, in a broader sense. One is just the idea that childhood matters, that what happens early on has a shape and a logic to it, and that it's worth paying attention to. Freud was really one of the first people to take seriously the idea that children have an inner life that's different from adults' and that's worth studying on its own terms. Before that, the dominant view was more that children were just small, defective adults.

The other thing, which I think is actually quite deep, is this idea that a lot of what's going on in the mind isn't accessible to consciousness. Now, Freud's version of the unconscious was this dramatic, repressed, seething thing, and the modern cognitive science version is much more boring — it's just that most of the computation your brain is doing, you don't have introspective access to. But the basic insight that the mind is doing much more than you can report on is right, and it's especially right for children. A two-year-old is doing extraordinarily sophisticated statistical inference and causal learning and theory-of-mind reasoning, and they have no idea they're doing it. You can't just ask them. You have to design clever experiments to find out.

And I'd add one more, which is that Freud was interested in play and fantasy and dreams, in the imaginative side of children's lives, and took it seriously as something meaningful rather than just noise. I think he got the meaning wrong, mostly. But the instinct that pretend play is telling you something important about how the mind works — that's one I share.

astra-6.text:
I think the broad idea that things that happen to you early in childhood can influence you later, without your being aware of that influence, has held up. And the idea that much of what goes on in our minds isn’t conscious has certainly held up. But those are very general ideas. The specific Freudian story about childhood—the sexual stages, the Oedipus complex—really hasn’t been supported by the evidence.

One of the striking things about Freud is that his account of childhood came largely from adults looking back, rather than from studying children themselves. When you actually look at young children, what you see is much more learning, exploration, and figuring out how the world works than you would expect from reading Freud.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the broad idea that what happens in childhood can shape us in ways that we don’t consciously understand has held up. And the idea that much of what goes on in our minds is unconscious has certainly held up, although the unconscious that cognitive scientists talk about looks very different from Freud’s.

What hasn’t held up very well are the specific stories about childhood sexuality and the particular stages that children are supposed to go through. One of the difficulties is that Freud was largely reconstructing childhood from what adults said in analysis, rather than actually studying children. When you look directly at children, you find a much richer picture of what they’re thinking and learning.
